title: Don’t Yell At Students udents/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts witnessing a fellow teacher on a field trip repeatedly yelling at her class to control their behavior, with only fleeting and temporary results, and uses the story to introduce a broader argument against raising one's voice as a management tool. He lists five reasons teachers yell -- not knowing a better way, distrust of their own plan, inconsistent rule enforcement, taking misbehavior personally, and short-term effectiveness -- and argues that all five point back to inadequate classroom management rather than any real benefit to yelling. He contends that yelling actually trains students to tune out a normal speaking voice, since they come to believe volume signals how much a teacher truly means what is said, and that it also models a loss of control for students to imitate. The piece frames a calm, consistently enforced classroom management plan as a complete substitute for yelling, one that communicates expectations clearly without relying on intimidation. Linsin closes with a direct challenge to readers to resolve never to raise their voice and instead rely entirely on consistent enforcement of stated consequences.
points: Yelling teaches students that a teacher only 'means it' when volume is raised, which paradoxically makes a normal speaking voice less effective over time.

Five common causes of yelling are identified -- not knowing a better way, distrust of one's plan, inconsistent enforcement, taking behavior personally, and short-term apparent effectiveness -- all traced back to weak classroom management.
Yelling models a loss of control for students, teaching them how to react when things don't go their way.
A calm, consistently enforced classroom management plan is presented as a full substitute for raising one's voice, creating a 'safe world that makes sense' for students.
Yelling is contrasted with lecturing as another ineffective substitute for genuine classroom management discipline.
quotes: Anthony! Get your hands off the glass right now! And Taylor! I said to walk!” The teacher accompanying the class of excitable students just ahead of us was reacting to every misdeed with the screech of her voice.
Teachers yell at students for one or more of the following reasons: 1. They don’t know a better way. 2. They don’t trust their classroom management plan.
Whenever you raise your voice, you’re communicating to your students that you only mean what you say when you yell. And to them, the louder you are, the more you mean it.

Yelling also shows a loss of control, which provides a poor model for your students. When you yell or fail to conceal your frustrations in front of them, you’re teaching your students how to behave when things don’t go their way.
Yelling, on the other hand, creates distrust and resentment in students because it’s arbitrary, it’s based on intimidation, and it chisels away at a child’s dignity.

Resolve to never raise your voice in response to misbehavior, and instead, focus on clearly communicating your boundaries of behavior to your students and then enforcing those boundaries 100% of the time.
